body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Blood plasma contains ...

A. Platelets
B. Albumin
C. Reticulocytes
D. Fibrinogen
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Platelets | **F** | Platelets are formed elements suspended **in** plasma, not a plasma constituent. |
| B. Albumin | **T** | Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein. |
| C. Reticulocytes | **F** | Reticulocytes are young red cells, a formed element. |
| D. Fibrinogen | **T** | Fibrinogen is a plasma protein (plasma minus fibrinogen and clotting factors = serum). |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Whole blood = **formed elements** (red cells, reticulocytes, leucocytes, platelets) suspended in **plasma**. Plasma is ~92% water plus proteins (albumin, globulins, **fibrinogen**), electrolytes, nutrients, hormones and wastes. When blood clots, fibrinogen is consumed, so **serum** lacks fibrinogen.

## Simplified explanation

Plasma is the liquid part of blood. Proteins like albumin and fibrinogen are dissolved in it; cells and platelets float in it but are not part of it.
hint: Separate the liquid (plasma) from the cells floating in it.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Excess erythrocyte production may occur in conditions of ...

A. Defective HIF 1α production
B. Defective von Hippel Lindau protein production
C. Defective prolyl hydroxylase enzyme production
D. Defective pulmonary function
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Defective HIF 1α production | **F** | Without HIF-1α the erythropoietin gene is not switched on, so EPO and red-cell output fall. |
| B. Defective von Hippel Lindau protein production | **T** | VHL tags HIF-α for destruction; without it HIF accumulates and EPO rises (e.g. Chuvash polycythaemia). |
| C. Defective prolyl hydroxylase enzyme production | **T** | Prolyl hydroxylase (PHD2) marks HIF-α for VHL binding; loss stabilises HIF and raises EPO. |
| D. Defective pulmonary function | **T** | Chronic hypoxia from lung disease drives EPO and causes secondary polycythaemia. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In normoxia, **prolyl hydroxylases** hydroxylate HIF-α, which is then bound by the **von Hippel-Lindau (VHL)** E3 ubiquitin ligase and degraded. In hypoxia, hydroxylation stops, HIF-α pairs with HIF-β and switches on the **EPO** gene in renal peritubular cells. Loss of VHL or PHD function, or true tissue hypoxia (lung disease, high altitude), therefore increases EPO and red cell mass. Loss of HIF itself does the opposite.

## Simplified explanation

Low oxygen turns on HIF, and HIF turns on EPO. Anything that keeps HIF switched on (broken VHL, broken prolyl hydroxylase, poor lungs) makes too many red cells. No HIF means no EPO.
hint: Trace the oxygen-sensing pathway: PHD → VHL → HIF → EPO.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Totipotent stem cells include ...

A. Hair stem cells
B. Haematopoietic stem cells
C. Neuronal stem cells
D. Mesenchymal stromal cells
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Hair stem cells | **F** | Adult tissue stem cell: multipotent/unipotent at most. |
| B. Haematopoietic stem cells | **F** | HSCs are multipotent: they make all blood cells only. |
| C. Neuronal stem cells | **F** | Multipotent: neurons and glia only. |
| D. Mesenchymal stromal cells | **F** | Multipotent: bone, cartilage, fat, stroma. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Totipotent** cells (zygote up to the early morula) can form every embryonic **and** extra-embryonic tissue (placenta). **Pluripotent** cells (inner cell mass, embryonic stem cells) form all three germ layers. Adult stem cells, including HSCs, neural, hair-follicle and mesenchymal stromal cells, are **multipotent** or unipotent.

## Simplified explanation

Only the fertilised egg and its first few divisions are totipotent. All the cells listed are adult stem cells, which can only make a limited set of cell types, so all are false.
hint: Totipotent means able to make a whole organism, including the placenta.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The characteristic features of developing erythroblasts include ...

A. Haemoglobinization begins at the orthochromatophilic stage
B. Enucleation occurs at the reticulocyte stage
C. Proerythroblast are granulated
D. Reticulocytes lack protein synthesis ability
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Haemoglobinization begins at the orthochromatophilic stage | **F** | Haemoglobin becomes visible earlier, at the polychromatic stage (synthesis starts even earlier). |
| B. Enucleation occurs at the reticulocyte stage | **F** | The **orthochromatic** normoblast extrudes its nucleus; the product is the reticulocyte. |
| C. Proerythroblast are granulated | **F** | The proerythroblast has deep blue, agranular cytoplasm. |
| D. Reticulocytes lack protein synthesis ability | **F** | Reticulocytes still contain ribosomal RNA and keep making haemoglobin for 1–2 days. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Sequence: **pronormoblast → basophilic → polychromatic → orthochromatic normoblast → reticulocyte → erythrocyte**. Cytoplasm changes from blue (ribosomes) to grey-pink (polychromasia: RNA + Hb) to pink (Hb). Haemoglobin is first visible at the **polychromatic** stage. The **orthochromatic** normoblast ejects its nucleus (taken up by macrophages), leaving a reticulocyte that still has RNA and synthesises Hb. Erythroid precursors are agranular.

## Simplified explanation

Haemoglobin shows up before the last nucleated stage, the nucleus is pushed out by the orthochromatic normoblast (not the reticulocyte), red-cell precursors have no granules, and reticulocytes can still make protein. So all four are false.
hint: Recall the order of the normoblast stages and when Hb appears.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Effective haematopoiesis requires nutrients; the sources of various nutrients include ...

A. Lemon that is rich in iron
B. Leafy green vegetables that is rich in vitamin B12
C. Tea that enhances iron absorption
D. Legumes that is rich in iron
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Lemon that is rich in iron | **F** | Lemon supplies **vitamin C**, which aids iron absorption; it is not an iron source. |
| B. Leafy green vegetables that is rich in vitamin B12 | **F** | Leafy greens are rich in **folate**; vitamin B12 comes from animal foods. |
| C. Tea that enhances iron absorption | **F** | Tea **tannins** chelate non-haem iron and reduce absorption. |
| D. Legumes that is rich in iron | **T** | Beans, lentils and peas are good sources of non-haem iron. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Key haematinics: **iron** (haem iron in meat/fish/liver; non-haem iron in legumes, leafy greens), **vitamin B12** (only animal products: meat, liver, eggs, dairy), **folate** (leafy green vegetables, liver, legumes; destroyed by overcooking). **Ascorbic acid** reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ and promotes absorption; **tannins (tea)**, phytates and calcium inhibit it.

## Simplified explanation

Lemon helps you absorb iron, greens give folate, tea blocks iron uptake, and beans give iron. Only D is true.
hint: Think of what each food is actually rich in.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Transcription factors that instruct red cell/erythrocyte lineage formation include ...

A. EBF
B. E2A
C. FOG-1
D. CEBPα
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. EBF | **F** | Early B-cell factor drives B-lymphocyte commitment. |
| B. E2A | **F** | E2A is a B-lymphoid transcription factor. |
| C. FOG-1 | **T** | Friend of GATA-1 is the GATA-1 cofactor needed for erythroid (and megakaryocytic) maturation. |
| D. CEBPα | **F** | C/EBPα drives granulocytic differentiation. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Lineage choice is set by transcription factors: **GATA-1 + FOG-1, KLF1 (EKLF)** for erythroid cells; **GATA-1/FOG-1, FLI-1** for megakaryocytes; **PU.1** (high) for monocytes and **C/EBPα/ε** for granulocytes; **E2A, EBF, PAX5** for B cells; **GATA-3, Notch** for T cells.

## Simplified explanation

FOG-1 works with GATA-1 to make red cells. EBF and E2A make B cells; C/EBPα makes granulocytes.
hint: Match each factor with the lineage it is known for.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Neutrophils and eosinophils are both granulocytic cells. The differences include ...

A. eosinophils do not have a promyelocyte stage during its differentiation
B. eosinophils have only primary granules whereas neutrophils have both primary and secondary granules
C. eosinophilic granules are blue-black when stained with Leishman stain
D. eosinophil formation requires IL-5 whereas neutrophil formation does not
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. eosinophils do not have a promyelocyte stage during its differentiation | **F** | Both lineages pass through myeloblast → promyelocyte → myelocyte stages. |
| B. eosinophils have only primary granules whereas neutrophils have both primary and secondary granules | **F** | Eosinophils also have primary and specific (secondary, crystalloid) granules. |
| C. eosinophilic granules are blue-black when stained with Leishman stain | **F** | Eosinophil granules stain orange-red; blue-black granules are basophilic. |
| D. eosinophil formation requires IL-5 whereas neutrophil formation does not | **T** | IL-5 is the key eosinophil growth factor; neutrophils depend on G-CSF. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Both granulocytes arise from the CFU-GM/myeloid progenitor and mature through the same morphological stages. Eosinophils have **specific crystalloid granules** containing major basic protein, which bind **eosin** (orange). Their production is driven by **IL-5** (with IL-3, GM-CSF), whereas neutrophil production is driven mainly by **G-CSF**.

## Simplified explanation

Eosinophils go through the same stages as neutrophils and have both kinds of granules, which stain orange. The real difference is that eosinophils need IL-5.
hint: Think about the growth factor for each cell.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

MLS Asante prepared a stain by combining azure B and eosin Y dyes. If he uses this to stain peripheral blood thin smear, ...

A. azure B is anionic
B. azure B will bind to basic components of the cytoplasm
C. eosin Y is cationic
D. eosin Y will bind to the nuclear material
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. azure B is anionic | **F** | Azure B is a **basic (cationic)** dye. |
| B. azure B will bind to basic components of the cytoplasm | **F** | Azure B binds **acidic** components (DNA, RNA, basophil granules). |
| C. eosin Y is cationic | **F** | Eosin Y is an **acidic (anionic)** dye. |
| D. eosin Y will bind to the nuclear material | **F** | Eosin binds **basic** components such as haemoglobin and eosinophil granules. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In Romanowsky stains the **cationic** thiazine dye **azure B** binds anionic groups: phosphate of DNA/RNA (nuclei, blue cytoplasm) and sulphated heparin of basophil granules. The **anionic** dye **eosin Y** binds cationic groups: haemoglobin and the arginine-rich major basic protein of eosinophil granules. The purple of nuclei (Romanowsky effect) comes from an azure B-eosin complex on DNA.

## Simplified explanation

Azure B is a positive (basic) dye and sticks to acidic things like nuclei. Eosin is a negative (acidic) dye and sticks to basic things like haemoglobin. Every statement has it backwards, so all are false.
hint: Opposite charges attract: basic dyes stain acidic structures.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

During thrombopoiesis ...

A. Platelet quantitative output is inversely related to the megakaryocyte size
B. Platelet quantitative output is directly related to megakaryocyte nuclear content
C. Megakaryocyte size decreases with maturity
D. A third of platelet output is retained as storage pool in the bone marrow
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Platelet quantitative output is inversely related to the megakaryocyte size | **F** | Bigger megakaryocytes produce **more** platelets. |
| B. Platelet quantitative output is directly related to megakaryocyte nuclear content | **T** | Higher ploidy (more endomitosis) means more cytoplasm and more platelets. |
| C. Megakaryocyte size decreases with maturity | **F** | Megakaryocytes **enlarge** as they mature (endomitosis, cytoplasmic expansion). |
| D. A third of platelet output is retained as storage pool in the bone marrow | **F** | About one third of platelets is pooled in the **spleen**. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Megakaryocytes undergo **endomitosis** (DNA replication without cell division) to 8N–64N; cell size and cytoplasmic volume rise with ploidy, and each megakaryocyte sheds ~1000–5000 platelets via proplatelets, so output is proportional to size and nuclear content. Of circulating platelets, about **one third is reversibly sequestered in the spleen**.

## Simplified explanation

As megakaryocytes mature they get bigger and more nuclear material, and bigger ones make more platelets. The spare third of platelets sits in the spleen, not the marrow.
hint: Endomitosis makes megakaryocytes bigger, not smaller.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The features expected in a neutrophil from an individual suffering from left shift neutrophilia includes ...

A. Döhle bodies
B. Pappenheimer granules
C. Toxic granulation
D. Howell-Jolly bodies
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Döhle bodies | **T** | Seen in reactive (infective/inflammatory) neutrophilia. |
| B. Pappenheimer granules | **F** | Iron granules in **red cells**, not neutrophils. |
| C. Toxic granulation | **T** | Coarse dark primary granules typical of reactive left shift. |
| D. Howell-Jolly bodies | **F** | DNA remnants in **red cells** (e.g. hyposplenism). |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **left shift** (bands, metamyelocytes, myelocytes in blood) is typical of acute bacterial infection and inflammation. The accompanying **toxic changes** in neutrophils are toxic granulation, **Döhle bodies** (pale blue rough-ER remnants), and cytoplasmic vacuolation. Pappenheimer bodies and Howell-Jolly bodies are red cell inclusions.

## Simplified explanation

In infection, neutrophils show toxic granules and Döhle bodies. Pappenheimer and Howell-Jolly bodies are found in red cells.
hint: Which of these inclusions are found in neutrophils rather than red cells?

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Platelets ...

A. Are granulated
B. Are nucleated
C. Have mitochondria
D. Stains purple due to presence of thrombopoietin
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Are granulated | **T** | They contain α-granules, dense granules and lysosomes. |
| B. Are nucleated | **F** | Platelets are anucleate fragments of megakaryocyte cytoplasm. |
| C. Have mitochondria | **T** | Platelets have mitochondria for energy metabolism. |
| D. Stains purple due to presence of thrombopoietin | **F** | Their purple granules are azurophilic granule contents, not TPO; TPO is a hormone from the liver. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Platelets (2–4 µm) are anucleate but metabolically active: they contain **mitochondria**, glycogen, an open canalicular system, dense tubular system, and **α-granules** (fibrinogen, vWF, PF4, PDGF), **dense granules** (ADP, ATP, Ca²⁺, serotonin) and lysosomes. Their purple-red granularity on Romanowsky stains reflects these granules. **Thrombopoietin** is produced mainly by the liver and binds the platelet/megakaryocyte receptor c-Mpl.

## Simplified explanation

Platelets have no nucleus but do have granules and mitochondria. Their purple colour comes from the granules, not thrombopoietin.
hint: Platelets are cell fragments but still have organelles.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Platelet dense granules contains ...

A. vWF
B. fibrinogen
C. cathepsin
D. calcium
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. vWF | **F** | von Willebrand factor is stored in α-granules. |
| B. fibrinogen | **F** | Fibrinogen is in α-granules. |
| C. cathepsin | **F** | Cathepsins are lysosomal (λ-granule) enzymes. |
| D. calcium | **T** | Dense (δ) granules hold Ca²⁺, ADP, ATP and serotonin. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Dense (δ) granules**: ADP, ATP, **Ca²⁺**, serotonin (5-HT), pyrophosphate. **α-granules**: fibrinogen, vWF, factor V, PF4, β-thromboglobulin, PDGF, P-selectin. **Lysosomes**: acid hydrolases, cathepsins.

## Simplified explanation

Dense granules carry small molecules: ADP, ATP, calcium and serotonin. Proteins like vWF and fibrinogen are in α-granules.
hint: Dense granules carry small molecules, not large proteins.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Peripheral blood thrombocytosis may be caused by ...

A. Splenomegaly
B. Iron deficiency anaemia
C. Megaloblastic anaemia
D. Haemorrhage
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Splenomegaly | **F** | An enlarged spleen pools more platelets, causing thrombocytopenia. |
| B. Iron deficiency anaemia | **T** | A classic cause of reactive thrombocytosis. |
| C. Megaloblastic anaemia | **F** | Ineffective haematopoiesis usually lowers the platelet count. |
| D. Haemorrhage | **T** | Acute and chronic bleeding cause reactive thrombocytosis. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Reactive (secondary) thrombocytosis follows **iron deficiency, haemorrhage**, infection, inflammation, malignancy and **splenectomy**. **Splenomegaly** causes thrombocytopenia through hypersplenic pooling. **Megaloblastic anaemia** causes pancytopenia from ineffective haematopoiesis.

## Simplified explanation

Bleeding and iron deficiency push the platelet count up. A big spleen traps platelets, and B12/folate deficiency lowers them.
hint: Big spleen traps platelets; bleeding stimulates them.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Left shift neutrophilia implies presence of ...

A. megaloblastoid cells in peripheral blood smear
B. hypogranulated neutrophils in peripheral blood
C. Neutrophils with no nuclear segmentation
D. >50% bilobed neutrophils in peripheral blood
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. megaloblastoid cells in peripheral blood smear | **F** | Megaloblastoid change relates to B12/folate deficiency or dysplasia. |
| B. hypogranulated neutrophils in peripheral blood | **F** | Hypogranularity is a dysplastic feature; reactive shift gives toxic (heavy) granulation. |
| C. Neutrophils with no nuclear segmentation | **T** | Band forms and metamyelocytes have unsegmented nuclei. |
| D. >50% bilobed neutrophils in peripheral blood | **F** | Predominantly bilobed neutrophils suggest Pelger-Huët anomaly. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **left shift** means increased immature neutrophils in blood, chiefly **band (stab) forms** with unsegmented, horseshoe-shaped nuclei, sometimes metamyelocytes and myelocytes. It reflects increased demand (bacterial infection, inflammation) and release from the marrow storage pool.

## Simplified explanation

Left shift means more young neutrophils whose nuclei are not yet divided into lobes (bands).
hint: Left = younger cells on the maturation chart.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Akwasi Mensah has been on corticosteroid therapy for the past three days. The effect this may have on his haematological parameters include ...

A. Neutrophilia
B. Lymphocytosis
C. Eosinophilia
D. Monocytosis
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Neutrophilia | **T** | Steroids release marrow neutrophils and reduce margination and tissue migration. |
| B. Lymphocytosis | **F** | Steroids cause **lymphopenia** (redistribution and apoptosis). |
| C. Eosinophilia | **F** | Steroids cause **eosinopenia**. |
| D. Monocytosis | **F** | Steroids cause **monocytopenia**. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Glucocorticoids raise the neutrophil count by **demargination**, increased release from the marrow storage pool and reduced egress into tissues. They lower **lymphocytes, eosinophils and monocytes** by redistribution to lymphoid tissue/bone marrow and by apoptosis.

## Simplified explanation

Steroids push neutrophils up and push lymphocytes, eosinophils and monocytes down.
hint: Steroids raise only one type of white cell.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The morphological changes that may occur when EDTA-anticoagulated blood is stored at room temperature for 12 hours include ...

A. crenated red cells
B. sphering of red blood cells
C. vacuolization of red blood cells
D. lobulation of lymphocytes
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. crenated red cells | **T** | Echinocytes (crenation) develop with storage in EDTA. |
| B. sphering of red blood cells | **T** | Red cells gradually become spherocytic with storage. |
| C. vacuolization of red blood cells | **F** | Vacuolation affects neutrophils and monocytes, not red cells, which have no organelles. |
| D. lobulation of lymphocytes | **T** | Lymphocyte nuclei become lobulated or cleft (storage artefact). |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Storage artefacts of EDTA blood (worse at room temperature, after a few hours): **crenation** and progressive **sphering** of red cells (raised MCV), swelling and **vacuolation of neutrophils/monocytes**, nuclear **lobulation** of lymphocytes and pyknosis of neutrophils. Films should be made within ~3 hours of collection.

## Simplified explanation

Old EDTA blood shows crinkled and rounded red cells and lymphocytes with lobed nuclei. Vacuoles appear in white cells, not red cells.
hint: Red cells have no organelles to form vacuoles.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In Alder-Reilly anomaly; ...

A. Is sex-linked recessive disorder
B. Neutrophils are hypo-granular
C. Neutrophils are hypo-segmented
D. Neutrophils have defective chemotactic response
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Is sex-linked recessive disorder | **F** | Inheritance is autosomal recessive. |
| B. Neutrophils are hypo-granular | **F** | Neutrophils contain large, dark azurophilic (mucopolysaccharide) granules. |
| C. Neutrophils are hypo-segmented | **F** | Hyposegmentation is the Pelger-Huët anomaly. |
| D. Neutrophils have defective chemotactic response | **F** | Neutrophil function is normal. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Alder-Reilly anomaly** is an **autosomal recessive** finding linked to mucopolysaccharidoses (Hurler, Hunter, Maroteaux-Lamy): coarse dark-purple granules of partially degraded mucopolysaccharide appear in granulocytes (and sometimes lymphocytes/monocytes). Cell **function is normal**. It must not be mistaken for toxic granulation.

## Simplified explanation

In Alder-Reilly the neutrophils have extra-heavy dark granules, normal lobes and normal function, and it is autosomal recessive, so all are false.
hint: Alder-Reilly is about heavy granules, not lobes or function.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Platelet function is defective in ...

A. Chediak-Higashi syndrome
B. Alder-Reilley anomaly
C. Pelger-Huet anomaly
D. May-Hegglin anomaly
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Chediak-Higashi syndrome | **T** | Dense-granule (storage pool) deficiency causes a bleeding tendency. |
| B. Alder-Reilley anomaly | **F** | A granulation anomaly of leucocytes; platelets normal. |
| C. Pelger-Huet anomaly | **F** | Nuclear hyposegmentation only; platelets normal. |
| D. May-Hegglin anomaly | **F** | Giant platelets and thrombocytopenia, but platelet function is usually normal. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Chediak-Higashi syndrome** (LYST mutation) gives giant fused granules in leucocytes, partial albinism, immunodeficiency and a **platelet storage-pool (dense granule) deficiency** with prolonged bleeding. **May-Hegglin** (MYH9) has giant platelets and Döhle-like inclusions with mild thrombocytopenia, but platelet function is generally normal. Alder-Reilly and Pelger-Huët do not affect platelets.

## Simplified explanation

Only Chediak-Higashi damages platelet granules, so platelets work poorly.
hint: Which syndrome affects granules in many cell types?

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In Adults, neutrophil alkaline phosphatase score increases in conditions such as ...

A. Mumps infection
B. Bacterial infection
C. Acute inflammation
D. Chediak-Higashi syndrome
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Mumps infection | **F** | Viral infections usually do not raise the NAP score. |
| B. Bacterial infection | **T** | Activated neutrophils in bacterial infection have a high NAP score. |
| C. Acute inflammation | **T** | Inflammatory (leukaemoid) neutrophilia raises NAP. |
| D. Chediak-Higashi syndrome | **F** | Not a recognised cause of a raised NAP score. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**NAP (LAP) score** is **raised** in bacterial infection, inflammation, leukaemoid reaction, pregnancy/oral contraceptives, steroid therapy, polycythaemia vera and myelofibrosis. It is **low** in CML, PNH and some MDS. It is typically normal in viral infection, so it helps separate bacterial from viral causes and leukaemoid reaction from CML.

## Simplified explanation

Bacterial infection and acute inflammation activate neutrophils and push NAP up. Viral infections like mumps do not.
hint: NAP rises when neutrophils are activated against bacteria.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Migration of neutrophils in response to chemical gradients (chemotaxis) are cardinal in phagocytosis. Defective chemotactic response could occur as a result of ...

A. Corticosteroid therapy
B. Diabetes mellitus
C. Pelger-Huet anomaly
D. Leucoerythroblastosis
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Corticosteroid therapy | **T** | Steroids impair neutrophil adhesion and migration. |
| B. Diabetes mellitus | **T** | Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil chemotaxis and killing. |
| C. Pelger-Huet anomaly | **F** | Hyposegmented neutrophils function normally. |
| D. Leucoerythroblastosis | **F** | A blood picture (immature cells in blood), not a chemotactic defect. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Acquired chemotactic defects: **corticosteroids**, **diabetes mellitus**, alcohol, burns, malnutrition; inherited: leucocyte adhesion deficiency, Chediak-Higashi, hyper-IgE syndrome. **Pelger-Huët** neutrophils are functionally normal. **Leucoerythroblastosis** describes nucleated red cells and immature granulocytes in blood (marrow infiltration).

## Simplified explanation

Steroids and diabetes slow neutrophils down. Pelger-Huët cells work normally, and leucoerythroblastosis is a description of the blood film.
hint: Separate functional defects from morphological findings.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Antigens that are expressed on platelets include ...

A. MHC II
B. MHC I
C. AB antigens
D. Rh antigens
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. MHC II | **F** | MHC class II is on antigen-presenting cells, not platelets. |
| B. MHC I | **T** | Platelets carry HLA class I antigens (cause of refractoriness). |
| C. AB antigens | **T** | ABO antigens are present on platelets (intrinsic and adsorbed). |
| D. Rh antigens | **F** | Rh antigens are not expressed on platelets. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Platelets carry **HLA class I** (important in alloimmune platelet refractoriness), **ABH antigens**, and platelet-specific **HPA** antigens on glycoproteins (e.g. HPA-1a on GPIIIa). They lack HLA class II and **Rh** antigens (Rh is erythroid-specific).

## Simplified explanation

Platelets carry HLA class I and ABO antigens, but not HLA class II or Rh.
hint: Rh is a red-cell-only system.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

MLS Antiaye prepared and stained a thin blood smear. When the slide was examined using x100 oil immersion lens, the lymphocytes had 2 lobes. This ...

A. is a normal physiological finding
B. is due to bacterial infection
C. is due to viral infection
D. sample sat on the bench for long hours before film was prepared
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. is a normal physiological finding | **F** | Normal lymphocytes have round, non-lobed nuclei. |
| B. is due to bacterial infection | **F** | Bacterial infection affects neutrophils, not lymphocyte lobulation. |
| C. is due to viral infection | **F** | Viral infection gives reactive lymphocytes, not bilobed nuclei. |
| D. sample sat on the bench for long hours before film was prepared | **T** | Nuclear lobulation of lymphocytes is a storage artefact. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In EDTA blood stored for several hours at room temperature, lymphocyte nuclei become **lobulated or cleft**, neutrophils develop pyknosis and vacuoles, and red cells crenate. Films should be made within ~3 hours.

## Simplified explanation

Lobed lymphocytes on a film usually mean the blood was left standing too long before the film was made.
hint: Think artefact before disease.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The characteristics of reticulocytes includes ...

A. Ribosomes RNA
B. Protein synthetic ability
C. Being nucleated
D. Containing granules
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Ribosomes RNA | **T** | Residual ribosomal RNA forms the reticulum on supravital staining. |
| B. Protein synthetic ability | **T** | They continue haemoglobin synthesis for 1–2 days. |
| C. Being nucleated | **F** | Reticulocytes are anucleate. |
| D. Containing granules | **F** | They have no granules; the 'reticulum' is precipitated RNA seen only with supravital stains. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Reticulocytes are anucleate, slightly larger than mature red cells, contain residual **ribosomal RNA** (precipitated by new methylene blue/brilliant cresyl blue as a blue reticulum) and mitochondria, and continue to **synthesise haemoglobin**. They mature in marrow ~1–2 days and in blood ~1 day; on Romanowsky stain they appear as polychromatic cells.

## Simplified explanation

Reticulocytes are young red cells: no nucleus, but still some RNA, so they can still make haemoglobin.
hint: Reticulocyte = red cell that has just lost its nucleus.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Haematopoietic cells that are normally found in peripheral blood include ...

A. megakaryocyte
B. reticulocyte
C. plasma cell
D. nucleated red blood cells
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. megakaryocyte | **F** | Megakaryocytes stay in the marrow; only platelets circulate. |
| B. reticulocyte | **T** | Normally 0.5–2.5% of red cells in adults. |
| C. plasma cell | **F** | Plasma cells live in marrow and lymphoid tissue, not normal blood. |
| D. nucleated red blood cells | **F** | Normal only in neonates; in adults they indicate disease. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Normal adult blood contains erythrocytes, **reticulocytes** (0.5–2.5%), neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils and platelets. Megakaryocytes, plasma cells and nucleated red cells are marrow cells; their presence in blood is abnormal (except NRBCs in the newborn).

## Simplified explanation

Of the four, only reticulocytes normally circulate in adult blood.
hint: Which cell is counted in a routine reticulocyte count?

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The cells that form the erythroblastic islands includes ...

A. Monocytes
B. Megakaryocytes
C. Macrophages
D. Mast cells
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Monocytes | **F** | Circulating cells; not the central island cell. |
| B. Megakaryocytes | **F** | Not part of erythroblastic islands. |
| C. Macrophages | **T** | A central 'nurse' macrophage surrounded by erythroblasts. |
| D. Mast cells | **F** | Not part of erythroblastic islands. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

An **erythroblastic island** is a **central macrophage** surrounded by developing erythroblasts. The macrophage supplies iron (ferritin), growth signals and adhesion (EMP, VCAM-1/α4β1), and phagocytoses the extruded nuclei.

## Simplified explanation

Red-cell precursors cluster around a central macrophage that feeds them iron and eats their nuclei.
hint: A 'nurse cell' sits in the middle.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

If frothing occurs when venous blood sample is drawn, this can lead to ...

A. haemolysis
B. platelet activation
C. increased [haemoglobin]
D. increased platelet count
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. haemolysis | **T** | Turbulence and air bubbles rupture red cells. |
| B. platelet activation | **T** | Turbulence activates platelets (clumping). |
| C. increased [haemoglobin] | **F** | Haemolysis does not raise the total haemoglobin measured. |
| D. increased platelet count | **F** | Activated platelets clump, so the count is **falsely low**. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Frothing during venepuncture (poor needle fit, small needle, forceful aspiration) causes **haemolysis** and **platelet activation/clumping**. The result is a falsely low platelet count, possible small clots, and haemolysed plasma (raised K⁺, LDH). Total Hb is unchanged or slightly affected; it is not raised.

## Simplified explanation

Bubbles and turbulence burst red cells and make platelets stick together, so the platelet count drops.
hint: Clumped platelets are not counted.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Granulopoiesis; ...

A. Primary granules are formed at the myeloblast stage
B. Secondary granules are formed at the myelocyte stage
C. Mitotic pool includes myelocytes and metamyelocyte
D. Eosinophil formation occurs in the tonsils
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Primary granules are formed at the myeloblast stage | **F** | Primary (azurophilic) granules are formed at the **promyelocyte** stage. |
| B. Secondary granules are formed at the myelocyte stage | **T** | Specific (secondary) granules appear at the myelocyte stage. |
| C. Mitotic pool includes myelocytes and metamyelocyte | **F** | The mitotic pool is myeloblast, promyelocyte and myelocyte; metamyelocytes can no longer divide. |
| D. Eosinophil formation occurs in the tonsils | **F** | Eosinophils are made in the bone marrow. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Marrow granulocyte compartments: **mitotic (proliferating) pool**: myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte; **maturation/storage pool**: metamyelocyte, band, segmented neutrophil. **Primary (azurophilic) granules** containing MPO are synthesised in the **promyelocyte**; **secondary (specific)** granules (lactoferrin, lysozyme) begin in the **myelocyte**. All granulocytes, including eosinophils, are produced in the bone marrow.

## Simplified explanation

Primary granules come in at the promyelocyte, secondary granules at the myelocyte. Metamyelocytes can't divide any more, and eosinophils are made in the marrow.
hint: The myelocyte is the last cell that can divide.

body: Both red blood cells and neutrophils uses glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) enzyme in their metabolic adaptations. In not more than two sentences, explain the main differences in the end-products of the use of G6PD enzyme by these two haematopoietic cells.
answer:
In both cells G6PD (hexose monophosphate shunt) generates **NADPH**, but:

- **Red cells** use NADPH (via glutathione reductase) to keep **glutathione reduced (GSH)**, which detoxifies H₂O₂ and protects haemoglobin and the membrane from **oxidant damage**.
- **Neutrophils** use NADPH as the electron donor for **NADPH oxidase**, producing **superoxide, H₂O₂ and hypochlorous acid** (respiratory burst) to **kill ingested microbes**.

> [!answer]
> Red cell: NADPH → reduced glutathione → antioxidant protection. Neutrophil: NADPH → NADPH oxidase → reactive oxygen species for microbial killing.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

G6PD catalyses the first step of the pentose phosphate pathway: glucose-6-phosphate + NADP⁺ → 6-phosphogluconolactone + **NADPH**. The red cell has no other NADPH source; NADPH regenerates GSH, which with glutathione peroxidase removes H₂O₂ (G6PD deficiency → Heinz bodies, haemolysis). In the neutrophil, NADPH oxidase (gp91phox) transfers electrons from NADPH to O₂ to form O₂⁻, then H₂O₂ and, via myeloperoxidase, HOCl (deficient in chronic granulomatous disease; severe G6PD deficiency can mimic CGD).

## Simplified explanation

Both cells make NADPH with G6PD. Red cells use it to defend against oxidants; neutrophils use it to make oxidants that kill germs.
hint: Defence (red cell) versus attack (neutrophil).

body: In not more than one sentence explain why splenectomy adversely affects platelet count.
answer:
The spleen normally pools about **one third** of the body's platelets; after splenectomy this pool is released and platelet removal falls, so the count rises (**post-splenectomy thrombocytosis**).

> [!answer]
> Loss of the splenic platelet pool (~⅓ of platelets) causes thrombocytosis.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

About 30–35% of the platelet mass is sequestered in the splenic red pulp in equilibrium with blood; the spleen also removes aged platelets. Splenectomy releases this pool and reduces clearance, giving a reactive thrombocytosis (often >600 × 10⁹/L) that can persist and carries a thrombosis risk.

## Simplified explanation

The spleen stores a third of platelets. Take it out and they all stay in the blood, so the count goes up.
hint: Where is a third of the body's platelets normally kept?

body: In not more than one sentence, explain whether defective function of superoxide dismutase impact oxidant stress or not on red blood cells.
answer:
Yes: superoxide dismutase converts **superoxide (O₂⁻)** to H₂O₂ (then removed by catalase/glutathione peroxidase), so defective SOD lets superoxide accumulate, **increasing oxidant stress** and oxidative damage (methaemoglobin, Heinz bodies, haemolysis).

> [!answer]
> Yes, it increases oxidant stress because superoxide is no longer dismutated.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Red cells constantly generate O₂⁻ from Hb autoxidation (oxyHb → metHb + O₂⁻). **SOD** dismutes 2O₂⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O₂ + O₂; **catalase** and **glutathione peroxidase** (with GSH regenerated via NADPH from G6PD) remove H₂O₂. Failure at the SOD step leaves superoxide to oxidise haemoglobin and membrane lipids.

## Simplified explanation

SOD is the first clean-up enzyme for superoxide. If it fails, superoxide builds up and damages the red cell.
hint: SOD is the first antioxidant enzyme in the chain.

body: State two (2) characteristic features of neutrophils in leukaemoid reaction that makes them different from a neutrophil in a leukaemia.
answer:
Any two:

- **Toxic granulation**
- **Döhle bodies** and/or cytoplasmic **vacuolation**
- **High neutrophil alkaline phosphatase (NAP) score** (low in CML)
- Predominantly **mature** neutrophils and bands with few myelocytes/blasts

> [!answer]
> Toxic granulation/Döhle bodies and a high NAP score.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **leukaemoid reaction** is a reactive leucocytosis (>50 × 10⁹/L) to severe infection, haemorrhage or malignancy. The neutrophils are activated, so they show toxic changes and a **raised NAP**. In **CML**, NAP is low, toxic changes are absent, and there is a 'myelocyte bulge' with basophilia and the BCR-ABL1 fusion.

## Simplified explanation

In a leukaemoid reaction neutrophils look like they are fighting infection (toxic granules, Döhle bodies) and have a high NAP. Leukaemic neutrophils do not.
hint: Reactive neutrophils show signs of activation.

body: In not more than one sentence, explain why granules of basophils stain blue-black in a Romanowsky stain.
answer:
Basophil granules contain strongly **acidic (anionic) sulphated heparin** (and chondroitin sulphate), which binds the **basic (cationic) dye azure B/methylene blue**, staining them blue-black.

> [!answer]
> Acidic heparin in the granules binds the basic azure dye.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Romanowsky staining depends on charge: cationic thiazine dyes (azure B, methylene blue) bind anionic groups (phosphate, sulphate, carboxyl). Heparin is the most highly sulphated molecule in the body, so basophil granules bind azure B intensely and show **metachromasia** (purple-black).

## Simplified explanation

The granules are very acidic, so they soak up the blue basic dye.
hint: Acidic structures bind basic dyes.

body: In not more than two (2) sentences, explain how impaired von Hippel Lindau protein function will have on erythropoiesis.
answer:
VHL protein normally targets hydroxylated **HIF-α for ubiquitination and degradation** in normoxia; if VHL is impaired, HIF-α is stabilised even in normal oxygen, so **EPO is overproduced** and erythropoiesis is increased, causing **erythrocytosis/polycythaemia** (e.g. Chuvash polycythaemia).

> [!answer]
> HIF is not degraded → excess EPO → increased erythropoiesis (secondary polycythaemia).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Oxygen-dependent prolyl hydroxylases hydroxylate HIF-α; VHL (an E3 ligase component) binds hydroxylated HIF-α and sends it for proteasomal degradation. Homozygous VHL R200W (Chuvash) or VHL tumour syndromes stabilise HIF, raising EPO and causing a congenital/secondary erythrocytosis with high EPO.

## Simplified explanation

VHL normally destroys HIF. If VHL doesn't work, HIF stays switched on, the kidney makes more EPO and the marrow makes too many red cells.
hint: VHL is the 'off switch' for HIF.

body: State two (2) examples of a Romanowsky stain.
answer:
Any two: **Leishman**, **Giemsa**, **Wright**, **May-Grünwald-Giemsa**, **Jenner**, **Field's** stain.

> [!answer]
> Leishman and Giemsa (also Wright, May-Grünwald-Giemsa, Jenner, Field's).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Romanowsky stains combine a cationic thiazine dye (methylene blue and its oxidation products, especially **azure B**) with the anionic dye **eosin Y**, dissolved in methanol (fixative) and buffered at pH 6.8–7.2. Leishman, Giemsa, Wright, Jenner, May-Grünwald and Field's are all variants.

## Simplified explanation

Leishman and Giemsa are the two most common blood-film stains of this type.
hint: Think of the stains used for blood films and malaria.

body: In not more than one sentence, explain why the granules of eosinophils stain orange in a Romanowsky stain.
answer:
Eosinophil granules contain strongly **basic (cationic), arginine-rich proteins** such as **major basic protein**, which bind the **acidic (anionic) dye eosin**, staining them orange-red.

> [!answer]
> Basic proteins in the granules bind the acidic dye eosin.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Eosinophil specific granules have a crystalloid core of **major basic protein** plus eosinophil cationic protein, eosinophil peroxidase and eosinophil-derived neurotoxin. Their positive charge attracts the negatively charged eosin Y, giving the bright orange colour.

## Simplified explanation

The granules are full of basic proteins, so they pick up the orange acidic dye eosin.
hint: Basic structures bind acidic dyes.

body:
For each item, write the letter of the correct definition from the list (each definition can be used only once).

**Terms:** (i) Leucoerythroblastosis (ii) Basophilic stippling (iii) Thrombopoietin (iv) Myeloperoxidase (v) ADP (vi) Howell-Jolly bodies (vii) Anisocytosis (viii) Hypochromia (ix) Superoxide dismutase (x) 5-hydroxytryptamine (xi) PU.1 (xii) Fibrinogen (xiii) Poikilocytosis

**Definitions:**
A. Inhibitor of platelet aggregation
B. Activator of platelet aggregation
C. Transcription factor for erythropoiesis
D. Transcription inducing monopoiesis
E. Transcription factor inducing thrombopoiesis
F. Transcription factor inducing granulopoiesis
G. Induces hydrogen peroxide formation
H. Induces singlet oxygen formation
I. Red cells having reduced haemoglobin content
J. Varying red cell sizes
K. Varying red cell shapes
L. Presence of immature erythroid and granulocytic cells in peripheral blood
M. Clusters of cytoplasmic DNA in circulating erythrocytes
N. Clusters of cytoplasmic RNA in circulating erythrocytes
O. Iron granules in erythrocytes
P. Vasodilator
Q. Vasoconstrictor
R. Growth factor for platelet formation
S. Growth factor for erythrocyte formation
T. Binds to platelet glycoprotein Ia
U. Binds to platelet glycoprotein IIIa/IIb
V. Catalyses formation of hypochloric ion in neutrophils
answer:
| Term | Letter |
|---|---|
| Leucoerythroblastosis | **L** |
| Basophilic stippling | **N** |
| Thrombopoietin | **R** |
| Myeloperoxidase | **V** |
| ADP | **B** |
| Howell-Jolly bodies | **M** |
| Anisocytosis | **J** |
| Hypochromia | **I** |
| Superoxide dismutase | **G** |
| 5-hydroxytryptamine | **Q** |
| PU.1 | **D** |
| Fibrinogen | **U** |
| Poikilocytosis | **K** |

> [!answer]
> L, N, R, V, B, M, J, I, G, Q, D, U, K
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

- **Leucoerythroblastosis**: nucleated red cells + immature granulocytes in blood (marrow infiltration, fibrosis).
- **Basophilic stippling**: aggregated ribosomal **RNA** (lead poisoning, thalassaemia); **Howell-Jolly bodies** are **DNA** remnants (hyposplenism); Pappenheimer bodies are iron (O, unused).
- **Thrombopoietin** drives megakaryocyte/platelet production (R); EPO would be S.
- **Myeloperoxidase** converts H₂O₂ + Cl⁻ → HOCl.
- **ADP** (dense granules) activates aggregation via P2Y1/P2Y12.
- **SOD** converts superoxide to H₂O₂.
- **Serotonin (5-HT)** from dense granules is a vasoconstrictor.
- **PU.1** at high levels drives monocyte/macrophage differentiation (C/EBPα drives granulocytes).
- **Fibrinogen** bridges platelets through **GPIIb/IIIa** (αIIbβ3); collagen binds GPIa/IIa.
- **Anisocytosis** = variation in size; **poikilocytosis** = variation in shape; **hypochromia** = reduced Hb content (pale cells).

## Simplified explanation

Match each word to what it does: e.g. TPO makes platelets, ADP makes platelets stick, fibrinogen joins platelets through GPIIb/IIIa, anisocytosis means different sizes and poikilocytosis means different shapes.
hint: RNA stippling vs DNA Howell-Jolly bodies is a common trap.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The haematopoietic stem cells of a 60 years-old man are not identical to that of the same person when he was 1 year old. The changes that occur in the haematopoietic stem cells as a person ages include ...

A. Accumulation of telomerase
B. Accumulation of intracellular proteins
C. Enhanced DNA repair mechanism
D. Telomere elongation
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Accumulation of telomerase | **F** | Telomerase activity is low in HSCs and does not accumulate; telomeres shorten with age. |
| B. Accumulation of intracellular proteins | **T** | Aged HSCs accumulate damaged/aggregated proteins (loss of proteostasis). |
| C. Enhanced DNA repair mechanism | **F** | DNA damage accumulates because repair becomes less efficient. |
| D. Telomere elongation | **F** | Telomeres **shorten** with each division and with age. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Hallmarks of HSC ageing: **telomere attrition**, accumulation of **DNA damage** (declining repair), loss of **proteostasis** with accumulation of protein aggregates, mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS, epigenetic drift, and a **myeloid-biased**, less regenerative HSC pool with clonal haematopoiesis.

## Simplified explanation

Old stem cells have shorter telomeres, more DNA damage and pile up junk proteins. They do not gain telomerase or better DNA repair.
hint: Ageing means damage builds up and repair gets worse.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In the ontogeny of haematopoiesis ...

A. primitive haematopoiesis begins in the AGM
B. definitive haematopoiesis begins in the yolk sac
C. primitive haematopoiesis forms only erythrocytes
D. definitive haematopoiesis does not form macrophages
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. primitive haematopoiesis begins in the AGM | **F** | Primitive haematopoiesis begins in the **yolk sac** blood islands. |
| B. definitive haematopoiesis begins in the yolk sac | **F** | Definitive HSCs arise in the **aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM)** region. |
| C. primitive haematopoiesis forms only erythrocytes | **F** | It also yields macrophages and megakaryocytes, although nucleated erythrocytes dominate. |
| D. definitive haematopoiesis does not form macrophages | **F** | Definitive HSCs give rise to all lineages, including monocytes/macrophages. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Primitive** haematopoiesis starts in the extra-embryonic **yolk sac** (~day 16–19), producing large nucleated erythrocytes (embryonic Hb: Gower, Portland) plus macrophages and megakaryocytes. **Definitive** HSCs emerge from haemogenic endothelium of the **AGM** region (~week 4–5), then seed the **fetal liver** (main site from ~6 weeks to mid-gestation), spleen, and finally the **bone marrow**, which becomes the main site in late fetal life.

## Simplified explanation

The first blood cells come from the yolk sac; the true stem cells come from the AGM. Primitive blood also makes some macrophages and megakaryocytes, and true stem cells make every type of blood cell. So all four are false.
hint: Yolk sac = primitive; AGM = definitive.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Components of the bone marrow niche includes ...

A. Macrophages
B. Mesenchymal stromal cells
C. Osteoclasts
D. Endothelial cells
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Macrophages | **T** | Macrophages retain HSCs (e.g. via CXCL12-producing stroma) and form erythroblastic islands. |
| B. Mesenchymal stromal cells | **T** | CXCL12-abundant reticular and LepR⁺ stromal cells are core niche cells. |
| C. Osteoclasts | **T** | Endosteal niche: bone remodelling by osteoclasts releases Ca²⁺ and growth factors that regulate HSCs. |
| D. Endothelial cells | **T** | The perivascular (sinusoidal) niche is formed by endothelial cells. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The HSC **niche** has an **endosteal** component (osteoblasts, osteoclasts) and a **perivascular** component (sinusoidal **endothelial cells**, CXCL12/SCF-producing **mesenchymal stromal cells**, pericytes), plus **macrophages**, megakaryocytes, sympathetic nerves and adipocytes. They provide SCF, CXCL12, angiopoietin-1, TPO and adhesion molecules that maintain quiescence and self-renewal.

## Simplified explanation

The stem-cell 'home' in the marrow is built from bone cells, stromal cells, blood-vessel lining cells and macrophages, so all four are true.
hint: Think endosteal plus perivascular niches.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The functions of the Luebering-Rapoport pathway in red blood cells include ...

A. Generation of NADPH
B. Generation of 2ATP molecules
C. Conversion of glucose 6 phosphate to 6-phosphogluconate
D. Generation of 1,3 diphosphoglycerate
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Generation of NADPH | **F** | NADPH comes from the hexose monophosphate (pentose phosphate) shunt. |
| B. Generation of 2ATP molecules | **F** | The shunt **bypasses** the ATP-generating phosphoglycerate kinase step, so ATP is lost, not gained. |
| C. Conversion of glucose 6 phosphate to 6-phosphogluconate | **F** | That is the G6PD step of the pentose phosphate pathway. |
| D. Generation of 1,3 diphosphoglycerate | **F** | The shunt **consumes** 1,3-BPG to make 2,3-BPG. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In the **Rapoport-Luebering shunt**, bisphosphoglycerate mutase converts **1,3-BPG → 2,3-BPG**, and 2,3-BPG phosphatase converts it to 3-phosphoglycerate, rejoining glycolysis. Its function is to produce **2,3-BPG**, which binds deoxy-Hb and lowers O₂ affinity. The cost is the loss of one ATP per glucose diverted.

## Simplified explanation

This side-path of glycolysis exists to make 2,3-BPG. It does not make NADPH or ATP, and it uses up 1,3-BPG rather than making it, so all four are false.
hint: What is the one product this shunt is named for?

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The functions of 2,3-diphosphoglycerate in the function of red blood cells include ...

A. Conversion of methaemoglobin to haemoglobin
B. Increased oxygen affinity of haemoglobin
C. Maintaining of sulphydryl groups of red blood cell in their reduced form
D. Conversion of GSSG to GSH
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Conversion of methaemoglobin to haemoglobin | **F** | Done by NADH-cytochrome b5 (methaemoglobin) reductase. |
| B. Increased oxygen affinity of haemoglobin | **F** | 2,3-DPG **decreases** O₂ affinity (shifts the curve to the right). |
| C. Maintaining of sulphydryl groups of red blood cell in their reduced form | **F** | That is the job of reduced glutathione (GSH). |
| D. Conversion of GSSG to GSH | **F** | Glutathione reductase does this using NADPH. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

2,3-DPG binds in the central cavity between the β-chains of **deoxyhaemoglobin**, stabilising the T (tense) state, which **lowers O₂ affinity** and favours O₂ release to tissues (right shift). Methaemoglobin reduction (NADH-methaemoglobin reductase) and thiol protection (GSH, glutathione reductase with NADPH) are separate pathways.

## Simplified explanation

2,3-DPG helps haemoglobin let go of oxygen. The other jobs listed belong to other enzymes, so all four are false.
hint: 2,3-DPG has one main job in oxygen delivery.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In the membrane structure of red blood cells, **transmembrane proteins** that provide cytoskeletal support include ...

A. Ankyrin
B. Spectrin
C. Band 3 protein
D. Protein 4.2
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Ankyrin | **F** | Ankyrin is a **peripheral** (cytoplasmic) protein linking spectrin to band 3. |
| B. Spectrin | **F** | Spectrin is the **peripheral** cytoskeletal lattice under the membrane. |
| C. Band 3 protein | **T** | Band 3 spans the bilayer and anchors the skeleton via ankyrin/protein 4.2. |
| D. Protein 4.2 | **F** | Protein 4.2 is **peripheral**, stabilising the band 3-ankyrin link. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Red cell membrane = lipid bilayer + **integral (transmembrane) proteins** (band 3, glycophorins A/B/C, Rh proteins, aquaporin, GLUT1) + **peripheral skeletal proteins** (α/β-spectrin, ankyrin, protein 4.1, 4.2, actin, adducin, tropomyosin). **Vertical** links: band 3–ankyrin–β-spectrin (with 4.2) and glycophorin C–protein 4.1. **Horizontal** links: spectrin dimer–dimer and spectrin–actin–4.1 junctional complexes.

## Simplified explanation

Only band 3 crosses the membrane; ankyrin, spectrin and protein 4.2 sit underneath it. (Glycophorins are also transmembrane.)
hint: Which protein actually crosses the lipid bilayer?

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In the membrane red blood cell, ...

A. Horizontal interaction is conferred by Ankyrin-to-alpha spectrin interaction
B. Sialic acid is anchored on band 3 proteins
C. Membrane cholesterol is in equilibrium with plasma cholesterol
D. Presence of Band 4.2 proteins confers a net negative charge to red blood cells
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Horizontal interaction is conferred by Ankyrin-to-alpha spectrin interaction | **F** | Ankyrin binds **β**-spectrin and is a **vertical** interaction. |
| B. Sialic acid is anchored on band 3 proteins | **F** | Sialic acid is carried mainly on **glycophorins**. |
| C. Membrane cholesterol is in equilibrium with plasma cholesterol | **T** | Red cell cholesterol exchanges freely with plasma (e.g. target cells in liver disease). |
| D. Presence of Band 4.2 proteins confers a net negative charge to red blood cells | **F** | The negative charge (zeta potential) comes from sialic acid on glycophorins. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Vertical** interactions (bilayer to skeleton): band 3–ankyrin–β-spectrin, protein 4.2, glycophorin C–4.1R; defects cause hereditary spherocytosis. **Horizontal** interactions (within the skeleton): spectrin heterodimer self-association and spectrin–actin–protein 4.1; defects cause elliptocytosis/pyropoikilocytosis. **Sialic acid** on glycophorins gives the red cell its negative surface charge (zeta potential). Membrane **cholesterol** equilibrates with plasma lipoproteins, so raised plasma cholesterol/bile acids (obstructive jaundice) expands the membrane and forms target cells.

## Simplified explanation

Ankyrin makes vertical links, sialic acid sits on glycophorins and gives the negative charge, and red-cell cholesterol swaps with plasma cholesterol. Only C is true.
hint: Vertical = bilayer to skeleton; horizontal = within the skeleton.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In describing red cells on peripheral smear ...

A. Acanthocytosis refers to variation in cell shapes
B. Anisocytosis refers to cell sizes
C. Variation in cell staining is referred to as hypochromasia
D. Presence of sickle cell is referred to as acanthocytosis
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Acanthocytosis refers to variation in cell shapes | **F** | Variation in shape is **poikilocytosis**; acanthocytes are cells with irregular spiky projections. |
| B. Anisocytosis refers to cell sizes | **T** | Anisocytosis = variation in red cell size. |
| C. Variation in cell staining is referred to as hypochromasia | **F** | Variation in staining is **anisochromasia**; hypochromasia is reduced staining (low Hb). |
| D. Presence of sickle cell is referred to as acanthocytosis | **F** | Sickle cells are **drepanocytes**. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Terminology: **anisocytosis** (size variation), **poikilocytosis** (shape variation), **anisochromasia** (variation in staining), **hypochromia** (pale cells, increased central pallor, low MCH), **acanthocytes** (few irregular spicules; abetalipoproteinaemia, liver disease), **echinocytes** (regular crenation), **drepanocytes** (sickle cells).

## Simplified explanation

Aniso = size, poikilo = shape, hypochromia = pale. Sickle cells are called drepanocytes.
hint: Learn the Greek prefixes.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The primary granules of granulocytes contain ...

A. Lactoferrin
B. Acid phosphatase
C. Collagenase
D. Myeloperoxidase
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Lactoferrin | **F** | A marker of **secondary (specific)** granules. |
| B. Acid phosphatase | **T** | Primary (azurophilic) granules are lysosomal and contain acid hydrolases. |
| C. Collagenase | **F** | Collagenase is in **secondary** granules. |
| D. Myeloperoxidase | **T** | MPO is the marker enzyme of primary granules. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Primary (azurophilic)** granules (formed at the promyelocyte stage): **myeloperoxidase**, acid phosphatase and other acid hydrolases, elastase, cathepsin G, defensins, lysozyme. **Secondary (specific)** granules (myelocyte stage): **lactoferrin**, **collagenase**, lysozyme, vitamin B12-binding protein. **Tertiary** granules: gelatinase. The NAP enzyme is in secretory vesicles.

## Simplified explanation

Primary granules are lysosome-like: MPO and acid phosphatase. Lactoferrin and collagenase belong to secondary granules.
hint: MPO marks the primary granule; lactoferrin marks the secondary.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The storage pool of granulocytes includes ...

A. Promyelocytes
B. Myelocytes
C. Metamyelocytes
D. Blast cells
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Promyelocytes | **F** | Promyelocytes divide: mitotic (proliferating) pool. |
| B. Myelocytes | **F** | Myelocytes are the last dividing stage: mitotic pool. |
| C. Metamyelocytes | **T** | Non-dividing metamyelocytes, bands and segmented neutrophils form the maturation-storage pool. |
| D. Blast cells | **F** | Myeloblasts belong to the mitotic pool. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Marrow neutrophil compartments: **mitotic (proliferating) pool**: myeloblasts, promyelocytes, myelocytes (~3–5 days); **maturation-storage pool**: **metamyelocytes**, bands and segmented neutrophils (~5–7 days), a reserve of several days' supply released under stress (infection, steroids). Blood has a **circulating** and a **marginating** pool of roughly equal size.

## Simplified explanation

Cells that can no longer divide (from the metamyelocyte on) wait in the marrow as a store, ready for release.
hint: Storage = non-dividing cells.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Growth factors responsible for eosinophil formation include ...

A. Eosinopoietin
B. IL-6
C. G-CSF
D. M-CSF
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Eosinopoietin | **T** | Eosinopoietin is the old name for **IL-5**, the main eosinophil growth factor. |
| B. IL-6 | **F** | IL-6 is mainly an acute-phase and thrombopoietic cytokine. |
| C. G-CSF | **F** | G-CSF drives neutrophil production. |
| D. M-CSF | **F** | M-CSF drives monocyte/macrophage production. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Eosinophil production is driven by **IL-5** (historically 'eosinopoietin'), helped by IL-3 and GM-CSF, mainly from Th2 lymphocytes. G-CSF → neutrophils; M-CSF → monocytes; IL-6 → acute phase response, megakaryopoiesis.

## Simplified explanation

IL-5 (eosinopoietin) is the growth factor for eosinophils.
hint: Each CSF is named for the cell it makes.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Sources of haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) includes ...

A. Bone marrow in adults
B. Spleen in adults
C. Umbilical cord blood in at-term babies
D. Peripheral blood in adults
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Bone marrow in adults | **T** | The main HSC reservoir in adults. |
| B. Spleen in adults | **F** | The adult spleen is not a normal source of HSCs. |
| C. Umbilical cord blood in at-term babies | **T** | Cord blood is rich in HSCs and used for transplantation. |
| D. Peripheral blood in adults | **T** | Small numbers circulate, and G-CSF-mobilised peripheral blood is the commonest transplant source. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

HSCs for transplantation are collected from **bone marrow** (aspiration from the iliac crest), **peripheral blood** after mobilisation with G-CSF (± plerixafor) by apheresis, and **umbilical cord blood**. The adult spleen does not normally harbour HSCs (only in extramedullary haematopoiesis).

## Simplified explanation

Stem cells can be collected from bone marrow, from blood after G-CSF injections, and from cord blood, but not from the normal adult spleen.
hint: Think of the three sources used for stem-cell transplants.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Cells in the bone marrow niche includes ...

A. Macrophages
B. Osteoblasts
C. Osteoclasts
D. Mast cells
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Macrophages | **T** | Niche macrophages help retain HSCs. |
| B. Osteoblasts | **T** | Endosteal niche cells. |
| C. Osteoclasts | **T** | Bone remodelling by osteoclasts contributes to the endosteal niche. |
| D. Mast cells | **F** | Not a recognised structural component of the HSC niche. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The HSC niche comprises **endosteal** cells (osteoblasts, osteoclasts) and **perivascular** cells (sinusoidal endothelium, CXCL12/SCF-producing mesenchymal stromal cells), with macrophages, megakaryocytes, adipocytes and sympathetic nerve fibres. Mast cells are marrow residents but are not considered niche cells.

## Simplified explanation

The stem-cell niche is made of bone-lining cells, stromal and vessel cells and macrophages. Mast cells are not part of it.
hint: Endosteal and perivascular niches.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The differences between basophilic normoblast (BN) and orthochromatophilic normoblast (ON) includes ...

A. BN has a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N:C) ratio compared to ON
B. ON has more condensed nuclear chromatin compared to BN
C. BN has a high haemoglobin content compared to ON
D. ON lacks nucleus whereas BN has a nucleus
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. BN has a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N:C) ratio compared to ON | **T** | N:C falls as the nucleus condenses and shrinks. |
| B. ON has more condensed nuclear chromatin compared to BN | **T** | The ON nucleus is small and pyknotic. |
| C. BN has a high haemoglobin content compared to ON | **F** | Haemoglobin increases with maturity; the ON has the most. |
| D. ON lacks nucleus whereas BN has a nucleus | **F** | The ON still has a (pyknotic) nucleus; the reticulocyte is the first anucleate stage. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

As normoblasts mature: cell size ↓, **N:C ratio ↓**, chromatin becomes **more condensed** (pyknotic in ON), cytoplasm changes from deep blue (ribosomes) to pink (**haemoglobin ↑**). The **orthochromatic normoblast** is the last nucleated stage; it extrudes its nucleus to become a reticulocyte.

## Simplified explanation

Younger cells have bigger nuclei and less haemoglobin. The orthochromatic normoblast still has a small dark nucleus.
hint: The ON is the last nucleated stage.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Erythropoietin (EPO) ...

A. Is produced exclusively in kidneys in the unborn
B. Causes increased expression of BCL-2 in erythroblast
C. Increases apoptosis in burst-forming unit-erythroid (BFU-E) cells
D. Levels in peripheral blood is directly related to RBC count
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Is produced exclusively in kidneys in the unborn | **F** | In the fetus EPO comes mainly from the **liver**. |
| B. Causes increased expression of BCL-2 in erythroblast | **T** | EPO-R/JAK2/STAT5 signalling up-regulates anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins (BCL-xL). |
| C. Increases apoptosis in burst-forming unit-erythroid (BFU-E) cells | **F** | EPO **prevents** apoptosis of erythroid progenitors. |
| D. Levels in peripheral blood is directly related to RBC count | **F** | EPO is **inversely** related to red cell mass/Hb (high in anaemia). |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

EPO is a glycoprotein hormone made by renal peritubular interstitial cells in adults (~90%; liver ~10%) and mainly by the **fetal liver** before birth. Binding to EPO-R on CFU-E and late BFU-E activates **JAK2–STAT5**, inducing anti-apoptotic **BCL-xL (BCL-2 family)**, GATA-1 and transferrin receptor expression; it is primarily a **survival** factor. Its level rises as Hb falls (except in renal failure).

## Simplified explanation

EPO keeps young red cells alive by switching on anti-death proteins like BCL-2/BCL-xL. Before birth the liver makes it, and the lower the red cell count the more EPO you have.
hint: EPO is a survival signal; it is made in the fetal liver.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Processes that occur during erythroblast differentiation include ...

A. Haemoglobinization beginning at basophilic erythroblast stage
B. Enucleation at reticulocyte stage
C. Proliferation peaking at the polychromatophilic stage
D. Regulated organelle degradation in reticulocyte stage by lipoxygenase activity
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Haemoglobinization beginning at basophilic erythroblast stage | **F** | Haemoglobin first becomes evident at the polychromatic stage. |
| B. Enucleation at reticulocyte stage | **F** | The orthochromatic normoblast enucleates to become the reticulocyte. |
| C. Proliferation peaking at the polychromatophilic stage | **T** | The polychromatic normoblast is the last and most numerous dividing stage. |
| D. Regulated organelle degradation in reticulocyte stage by lipoxygenase activity | **T** | 15-lipoxygenase degrades mitochondrial membranes in maturing reticulocytes. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Pronormoblast → basophilic → **polychromatic** (last stage able to divide; the largest pool of dividing cells) → orthochromatic normoblast (**enucleates**) → reticulocyte → red cell. Haemoglobin becomes visible from the polychromatic stage. In the reticulocyte, mitochondria and ribosomes are removed by autophagy (NIX-dependent mitophagy) and **15-lipoxygenase**, which attacks organelle membranes.

## Simplified explanation

Red-cell precursors divide most at the polychromatic stage. Reticulocytes clear out their mitochondria using lipoxygenase.
hint: Which stage is the last that can divide?

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Reticulocytes ...

A. Have a larger surface area compared to red blood cells
B. Lack haemoglobin synthesizing ability
C. Count is indicative of the overall bone marrow haematopoietic activity
D. Are enucleated
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Have a larger surface area compared to red blood cells | **T** | They are larger and lose ~20% of membrane as they mature. |
| B. Lack haemoglobin synthesizing ability | **F** | They still synthesise Hb from residual mRNA. |
| C. Count is indicative of the overall bone marrow haematopoietic activity | **T** | The reticulocyte count reflects marrow erythropoietic output. |
| D. Are enucleated | **T** | Reticulocytes have no nucleus. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Reticulocytes are anucleate, ~20% larger than mature red cells (higher MCV), with excess membrane that is remodelled in the spleen. Residual ribosomal RNA allows **continued Hb synthesis**. The (corrected) reticulocyte count/index is the best simple measure of **effective erythropoiesis**.

## Simplified explanation

Reticulocytes are big young red cells with no nucleus that still make haemoglobin; counting them shows how hard the marrow is working.
hint: Reticulocytes = young, bigger, still making Hb.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In the metabolism of red blood cells ...

A. Embden-Meyerhof pathway maintains haemoglobin iron in +2 state
B. deficiency of glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase produces the similar symptoms as deficiency of glutathione reductase deficiency
C. 2,3-diphosphoglycerate functions to enhance O2 loading to haemoglobin molecule
D. Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase enzyme is required to generate 2,3-diphosphoglycerate
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Embden-Meyerhof pathway maintains haemoglobin iron in +2 state | **T** | Glycolysis supplies NADH for methaemoglobin (cytochrome b5) reductase. |
| B. deficiency of glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase produces the similar symptoms as deficiency of glutathione reductase deficiency | **T** | Both impair GSH regeneration, giving oxidant haemolysis. |
| C. 2,3-diphosphoglycerate functions to enhance O2 loading to haemoglobin molecule | **F** | 2,3-DPG promotes O₂ **unloading**. |
| D. Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase enzyme is required to generate 2,3-diphosphoglycerate | **F** | 2,3-DPG comes from the Rapoport-Luebering shunt (bisphosphoglycerate mutase). |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The **Embden-Meyerhof pathway** produces ATP and **NADH**; NADH is used by **methaemoglobin reductase** to keep haem iron as Fe²⁺. The **hexose monophosphate shunt** (G6PD) produces **NADPH**, which **glutathione reductase** uses to regenerate GSH; deficiency of either enzyme leaves red cells vulnerable to oxidants (Heinz bodies, haemolysis). **2,3-DPG** from the Rapoport-Luebering shunt reduces O₂ affinity.

## Simplified explanation

Glycolysis keeps iron in the ferrous form, G6PD and glutathione reductase work in the same antioxidant chain, and 2,3-DPG helps oxygen leave haemoglobin.
hint: Match each pathway to its product.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The functions of erythropoietin on erythroid precursors include ...

A. Activation of GATA-1 transcription factor expression
B. Increased expression of CD71 receptors
C. Increased expression of anti-apoptotic factors
D. Activation of CEBP-α transcription factors
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Activation of GATA-1 transcription factor expression | **T** | EPO signalling sustains GATA-1 expression/activity. |
| B. Increased expression of CD71 receptors | **T** | CD71 (transferrin receptor 1) rises to import iron for haem. |
| C. Increased expression of anti-apoptotic factors | **T** | e.g. BCL-xL via STAT5. |
| D. Activation of CEBP-α transcription factors | **F** | C/EBPα is a granulocytic transcription factor. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

EPO binding to EPO-R activates **JAK2/STAT5, PI3K/AKT and MAPK**, which promote survival (BCL-xL), proliferation and differentiation: up-regulation of **GATA-1**, **transferrin receptor (CD71)** and haem/globin synthesis. C/EBPα directs myeloid (granulocytic) differentiation and is not an EPO target.

## Simplified explanation

EPO turns on red-cell genes (GATA-1), iron uptake (CD71) and survival signals. C/EBPα belongs to granulocytes.
hint: Which factor belongs to a different lineage?

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Laboratory findings in May-Hegglin anomaly includes ...

A. thrombocytopenia
B. agranular platelet
C. prolonged bleeding time
D. impaired neutrophil phagocytic function
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. thrombocytopenia | **T** | Mild-moderate thrombocytopenia with giant platelets. |
| B. agranular platelet | **F** | Platelets are giant, not agranular. |
| C. prolonged bleeding time | **F** | Most patients have normal platelet function and bleeding time. |
| D. impaired neutrophil phagocytic function | **F** | Neutrophil function is normal despite Döhle-like inclusions. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**May-Hegglin anomaly** (MYH9-related disorder, autosomal dominant): **thrombocytopenia**, **giant platelets**, and Döhle-like basophilic inclusions (aggregated non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA) in neutrophils. Most patients are asymptomatic; platelet and neutrophil **function are normal**. Some MYH9 disorders have nephritis, deafness or cataracts.

## Simplified explanation

May-Hegglin gives few but giant platelets and blue inclusions in neutrophils; the cells still work normally.
hint: MYH9: big platelets, low count, normal function.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Non-disease conditions that can cause neutrophilia includes ...

A. exercise
B. electrical shock
C. pregnancy
D. burns
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. exercise | **T** | Demargination during exercise raises the count. |
| B. electrical shock | **T** | Physical stress causes neutrophilia. |
| C. pregnancy | **T** | Physiological neutrophilia of pregnancy. |
| D. burns | **T** | Tissue injury produces neutrophilia. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Neutrophilia occurs with physiological and physical stimuli: **exercise**, **pregnancy** and labour, the newborn, emotional stress, heat, cold, **electric shock**, trauma, surgery and **burns** (stress hormones and cytokines cause demargination and marrow release), as well as infection, inflammation, haemorrhage, malignancy and drugs.

## Simplified explanation

Exercise, pregnancy, electric shock and burns all push neutrophils out of storage, so all four are true.
hint: Stress and tissue injury raise the neutrophil count.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Causes of peripheral blood left shift neutrophilia includes ...

A. bacterial infections
B. corticosteroid therapy
C. acute haemorrhage
D. tissue necrosis
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. bacterial infections | **T** | The classic cause. |
| B. corticosteroid therapy | **T** | Steroids release cells from the marrow storage pool. |
| C. acute haemorrhage | **T** | Acute bleeding mobilises the marrow reserve. |
| D. tissue necrosis | **T** | e.g. myocardial infarction, trauma. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A neutrophilia with **left shift** (bands, metamyelocytes) occurs whenever the marrow storage pool is mobilised: **bacterial infection**, sepsis, **tissue necrosis** (infarction, burns, trauma), **acute haemorrhage** or haemolysis, and drugs such as **corticosteroids** and G-CSF.

## Simplified explanation

Infection, bleeding, tissue death and steroids all release young neutrophils from the marrow, so all four are true.
hint: What empties the marrow storage pool?

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Basophils ...

A. contain granules that stain orange-pink in Leishman stain
B. are tri-lobed
C. contain heparin in their granules
D. develops into macrophages in tissues
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. contain granules that stain orange-pink in Leishman stain | **F** | Basophil granules stain **deep purple/blue-black**. |
| B. are tri-lobed | **F** | The nucleus is usually bilobed/irregular and obscured by granules. |
| C. contain heparin in their granules | **T** | Heparin and histamine are the main granule contents. |
| D. develops into macrophages in tissues | **F** | **Monocytes** become macrophages; basophils have a tissue counterpart in mast cells but do not become macrophages. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Basophils (<1% of WBCs) have a bilobed or irregular nucleus obscured by large **purple-black** granules containing **heparin**, **histamine**, and other mediators; they carry high-affinity IgE receptors (FcεRI) and mediate immediate hypersensitivity.
