Orange-pink granules belong to eosinophils. Monocytes, not basophils, differentiate into macrophages.

## Simplified explanation

Basophils have dark purple granules full of heparin and histamine. Orange granules are eosinophils, and macrophages come from monocytes.
hint: Remember what is inside basophil granules.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In Pelger-Huet anomaly ...

A. neutrophils are hypersegmented
B. the inheritance is autosomal recessive
C. neutrophils have impaired chemotactic response
D. neutrophils have enhanced phagocytic activity
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. neutrophils are hypersegmented | **F** | They are **hyposegmented** (bilobed 'pince-nez' or round nuclei). |
| B. the inheritance is autosomal recessive | **F** | Inheritance is **autosomal dominant** (lamin B receptor gene). |
| C. neutrophils have impaired chemotactic response | **F** | Function is normal. |
| D. neutrophils have enhanced phagocytic activity | **F** | Function is normal, not enhanced. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Pelger-Huët anomaly** is an **autosomal dominant** defect of the **lamin B receptor**: heterozygotes have bilobed 'spectacle' (pince-nez) neutrophils with coarse chromatin; homozygotes have round nuclei. Neutrophil function is **normal**. **Pseudo-Pelger** cells occur in MDS, AML and with some drugs. The main importance is not to mistake the cells for a left shift.

## Simplified explanation

Pelger-Huët neutrophils have too few lobes, it is autosomal dominant, and the cells work normally. All four statements are false.
hint: Pelger = fewer lobes, normal function.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The laboratory findings in leukaemoid reaction includes ...

A. right shift granulocytic cells in peripheral blood
B. leucoerythroblastosis
C. presence of myeloblast in peripheral blood
D. reduced neutrophil alkaline phosphatase score
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. right shift granulocytic cells in peripheral blood | **F** | There is a **left** shift. |
| B. leucoerythroblastosis | **F** | Nucleated red cells with immature granulocytes point to marrow infiltration, not a leukaemoid reaction. |
| C. presence of myeloblast in peripheral blood | **F** | Blasts are rare or absent; cells are mostly mature neutrophils and bands. |
| D. reduced neutrophil alkaline phosphatase score | **F** | NAP score is **raised** (low in CML). |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **leukaemoid reaction** is a reactive leucocytosis (>50 × 10⁹/L) resembling leukaemia, due to severe infection, haemorrhage, haemolysis or malignancy. Findings: neutrophilia with a **left shift** (bands, metamyelocytes, a few myelocytes), **toxic granulation and Döhle bodies**, and a **high NAP score**. Basophilia, blasts and leucoerythroblastic features suggest CML or marrow infiltration instead.

## Simplified explanation

In a leukaemoid reaction you see lots of mature and band neutrophils (left shift), toxic changes and a high NAP. All four statements are false.
hint: Leukaemoid reaction is reactive, so NAP goes up.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Hypersegmented neutrophils ...

A. have 4 – 5 lobes
B. occurs in Vitamin B12 deficiency
C. occurs in chronic nephritis
D. occur in viral infections in children
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. have 4 – 5 lobes | **F** | Normal neutrophils have 2–5 lobes; hypersegmentation means ≥6 lobes, or >5% with 5 lobes. |
| B. occurs in Vitamin B12 deficiency | **T** | A classic early sign of megaloblastic anaemia. |
| C. occurs in chronic nephritis | **T** | Seen in uraemia/chronic renal failure. |
| D. occur in viral infections in children | **F** | Not a feature of viral infection. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Hypersegmentation (right shift)**: >5% of neutrophils with 5 lobes or any with ≥6 lobes. Causes: **vitamin B12 or folate deficiency** (megaloblastic anaemia, often the earliest sign), **uraemia/chronic renal disease**, iron deficiency, hereditary hypersegmentation, and drugs (methotrexate, hydroxycarbamide).

## Simplified explanation

Neutrophils with 6 or more lobes are seen in B12/folate deficiency and kidney failure. Having 4–5 lobes is normal.
hint: Right shift = too many lobes.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The enzymes that are responsible for detoxification in neutrophils during phagocytosis include ...

A. superoxide dismutase
B. catalase
C. NADPH oxidase
D. glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. superoxide dismutase | **T** | Converts toxic superoxide to H₂O₂. |
| B. catalase | **T** | Breaks H₂O₂ down to water and oxygen. |
| C. NADPH oxidase | **F** | It **generates** superoxide (the respiratory burst); it is not a detoxifying enzyme. |
| D. glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase | **F** | It supplies NADPH but does not itself detoxify oxidants. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

During the respiratory burst **NADPH oxidase** makes O₂⁻, which forms H₂O₂ and (with MPO) HOCl to kill microbes. To protect the neutrophil itself, **superoxide dismutase**, **catalase** and the glutathione system (glutathione peroxidase/reductase) detoxify leaking ROS. G6PD provides the NADPH for both oxidase and glutathione reductase but is not a detoxifying enzyme.

## Simplified explanation

SOD and catalase clean up harmful oxygen products. NADPH oxidase makes them, and G6PD just supplies fuel.
hint: Separate the enzymes that make ROS from those that destroy them.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The secondary granules of neutrophils ...

A. contain collagenase
B. are formed at the metamyelocyte stage
C. contain lysozyme
D. contain acid hydrolase
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. contain collagenase | **T** | A specific-granule enzyme. |
| B. are formed at the metamyelocyte stage | **F** | They first appear at the **myelocyte** stage. |
| C. contain lysozyme | **T** | Lysozyme is present in both primary and secondary granules. |
| D. contain acid hydrolase | **F** | Acid hydrolases are in the primary (azurophilic, lysosomal) granules. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Secondary (specific)** granules appear at the **myelocyte** stage and contain **lactoferrin, collagenase, lysozyme**, vitamin B12-binding protein (transcobalamin), and NADPH oxidase components (cytochrome b558). **Primary** granules contain MPO, acid hydrolases, elastase, defensins and also lysozyme.

## Simplified explanation

Secondary granules hold lactoferrin, collagenase and lysozyme and start at the myelocyte. Acid hydrolases sit in primary granules.
hint: Myelocyte = specific granules appear.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Basophilic granules stain blue-black in Leishman staining procedure due to its ...

A. acidic nature
B. alkaline nature
C. neutral nature
D. heparin constituent
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. acidic nature | **T** | Acidic granules bind the basic thiazine dyes. |
| B. alkaline nature | **F** | Alkaline (basic) structures bind eosin and stain orange. |
| C. neutral nature | **F** | Neutral granules (neutrophil specific granules) stain lilac. |
| D. heparin constituent | **T** | Highly sulphated heparin gives the strong acidity. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Leishman stain contains basic methylene blue/azure dyes and acidic eosin. Basophil granules contain **heparin** (heavily sulphated glycosaminoglycan) and are strongly **acidic**, so they bind the basic dyes intensely (blue-black, metachromatic). Eosinophil granules are basic and bind eosin.

## Simplified explanation

Basophil granules are acidic because of heparin, so they take up the blue basic dye.
hint: Acidic structures bind basic dyes.

body: In not more than two (2) sentences, explain the roles of transcription factors and growth factors in haematopoiesis.
answer:
- **Growth factors** (cytokines such as SCF, IL-3, GM-CSF, G-CSF, EPO, TPO) bind receptors on the cell surface of stem/progenitor cells and signal them to **survive, proliferate and differentiate** (and functionally activate mature cells).
- **Transcription factors** (e.g. GATA-1, PU.1, C/EBPα, GATA-2, RUNX1) are nuclear proteins that switch lineage-specific genes on or off and so **determine lineage commitment and the programme of differentiation**.

> [!answer]
> Growth factors are external signals for survival/proliferation/differentiation; transcription factors inside the nucleus decide which lineage the cell becomes.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Haematopoiesis is regulated extrinsically by **cytokines/growth factors** (from stroma, T cells, macrophages, liver, kidney) acting through receptors (JAK-STAT) mostly as survival and mitogenic signals, and intrinsically by **transcription factor networks**. Cross-antagonism (e.g. GATA-1 vs PU.1) enforces lineage choice: GATA-1/FOG-1/KLF1 → erythroid/megakaryocyte; PU.1, C/EBPα → myeloid; E2A/EBF/PAX5 → B cells.

## Simplified explanation

Growth factors are messages from outside that tell cells to grow and mature. Transcription factors inside the nucleus pick which type of blood cell the cell becomes.
hint: Outside signal vs inside gene switch.

body: In not more than two sentences explain why the balance between BAX and BCL-2 molecules expression is important in erythroblast during erythropoietic differentiation.
answer:
**BAX** is pro-apoptotic and **BCL-2** (and BCL-xL) is anti-apoptotic; their ratio decides whether an erythroblast **survives and matures or undergoes apoptosis**. This balance (regulated by EPO) controls the number of red cells produced, and too much BAX relative to BCL-2 gives **ineffective erythropoiesis**.

> [!answer]
> The BAX:BCL-2 ratio determines erythroblast survival vs apoptosis and hence red cell output.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

BAX oligomerises in the mitochondrial outer membrane, releasing cytochrome c and activating caspases; BCL-2/BCL-xL block this. EPO (via STAT5) induces BCL-xL, rescuing CFU-E/proerythroblasts from apoptosis; in hypoxia high EPO saves more progenitors (increased output), while low EPO lets surplus cells die. Excess apoptosis (e.g. thalassaemia, MDS) causes ineffective erythropoiesis.

## Simplified explanation

BAX tells the cell to die, BCL-2 tells it to live. The balance decides how many young red cells survive to become red cells.
hint: One promotes death, the other survival.

body: Erythropoietin stimulates erythropoiesis but cannot stimulate granulopoiesis. Briefly explain why this is so.
answer:
Only **erythroid progenitors** (mainly CFU-E and late BFU-E, pronormoblasts) express the **EPO receptor**; granulocytic progenitors lack EPO receptors, so they cannot respond to EPO.

> [!answer]
> EPO receptors are expressed on erythroid, not granulocytic, progenitors.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Cytokine action depends on **receptor expression**. EPO-R (a type I cytokine receptor signalling via JAK2) is expressed from the late BFU-E to the early normoblast, peaking at the CFU-E stage. Granulocyte progenitors express G-CSF and GM-CSF receptors instead.

## Simplified explanation

A hormone only works on cells that have its receptor. Granulocyte precursors have no EPO receptor.
hint: Think receptors.

body: In not more than two sentences explain the difference between totipotency and pluripotency as applied to stem cells.
answer:
- **Totipotent** stem cells (the zygote and early blastomeres) can give rise to **all cell types of the embryo and the extra-embryonic tissues** (placenta, membranes), i.e. a whole organism.
- **Pluripotent** stem cells (inner cell mass/embryonic stem cells, iPS cells) can form **all three germ layers** (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm) but **not extra-embryonic tissues**.

> [!answer]
> Totipotent = whole organism including placenta; pluripotent = all embryonic germ layers but not placenta.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Potency hierarchy: totipotent > pluripotent > multipotent (e.g. HSC: all blood cells) > oligopotent (e.g. common myeloid progenitor) > unipotent. Potency declines as development proceeds.

## Simplified explanation

Totipotent cells can make everything, even the placenta. Pluripotent cells can make every body tissue but not the placenta.
hint: The difference is the placenta.

body: In not more than one sentence explain why nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio (N:C) reduces during erythropoiesis.
answer:
As the erythroblast matures the **nucleus condenses and shrinks** (chromatin condensation, eventually pyknosis and extrusion) while the **cytoplasm accumulates haemoglobin**, so the N:C ratio falls.

> [!answer]
> Nuclear condensation/shrinkage with relative increase in Hb-filled cytoplasm.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Pronormoblast N:C ~8:1; basophilic ~6:1; polychromatic ~4:1; orthochromatic ~1:2 before enucleation. Transcription shuts down as chromatin condenses (histone deacetylation), preparing for enucleation.

## Simplified explanation

The nucleus gets smaller and denser while the cytoplasm fills with haemoglobin.
hint: What happens to the nucleus as the cell matures?

body: In not more than two sentences, explain the effect of excessive production of HIF-1α on erythropoiesis.
answer:
Excess HIF-1α (HIF) switches on the **erythropoietin gene** (and iron-absorption genes), so EPO levels rise and **erythropoiesis increases**, leading to **erythrocytosis/secondary polycythaemia**.

> [!answer]
> More HIF → more EPO → more red cells (polycythaemia).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

HIF-α/β heterodimers bind hypoxia response elements in the EPO enhancer; HIF also up-regulates DMT1, duodenal cytochrome b, transferrin and transferrin receptor to supply iron. Stabilised HIF (VHL or PHD2 mutations, HIF-2α gain-of-function) causes congenital erythrocytosis.

## Simplified explanation

HIF is the switch for EPO. Too much HIF means too much EPO and too many red cells.
hint: HIF controls the EPO gene.

body: In not more than two sentences, explain the role of NADPH in the maintenance of red cell functional integrity.
answer:
NADPH (from the G6PD/hexose monophosphate shunt) is used by **glutathione reductase** to regenerate **reduced glutathione (GSH)**, which with glutathione peroxidase removes H₂O₂ and keeps haemoglobin and membrane **sulphydryl groups reduced**. This protects the red cell from **oxidant damage** (Heinz bodies, membrane damage, haemolysis).

> [!answer]
> NADPH keeps glutathione reduced, protecting Hb and the membrane from oxidation.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The red cell's only source of NADPH is the pentose phosphate pathway. NADPH also stabilises catalase. In G6PD deficiency, oxidant stress (drugs, fava beans, infection) oxidises Hb to methaemoglobin and denatured Heinz bodies, which are removed in the spleen (bite cells), causing haemolysis.

## Simplified explanation

NADPH recharges glutathione, the red cell's antioxidant, so oxidants cannot damage haemoglobin or the membrane.
hint: Think glutathione.

body: In not more than two sentences explain why reticulocytes stain as polychromatophilic cells.
answer:
Reticulocytes contain both **residual ribosomal RNA**, which takes up the **basic (blue) dye**, and **haemoglobin**, which takes up the **acidic dye eosin**; the mixture gives a **blue-grey (polychromatic)** colour on a Romanowsky stain.

> [!answer]
> RNA (basophilic) + haemoglobin (acidophilic) = mixed blue-grey colour.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Polychromasia on a Romanowsky film corresponds to reticulocytes (especially young 'shift' reticulocytes) seen with supravital stains, where the RNA is precipitated as a blue reticulum.

## Simplified explanation

Reticulocytes still have some RNA (blue) and lots of haemoglobin (pink), so they look bluish-grey.
hint: Two dyes, two components.

body: In one sentence, explain the main difference between storage pool and marginating pool as relates to granulopoiesis.
answer:
The **storage pool** is the reserve of mature neutrophils (with bands and metamyelocytes) held in the **bone marrow** awaiting release, whereas the **marginating pool** is neutrophils already **in the blood vessels** loosely adherent to the endothelium of small vessels (not counted in the WBC count).

> [!answer]
> Storage pool = in the marrow; marginating pool = in blood, stuck to vessel walls.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Blood neutrophils are split roughly 50:50 between the **circulating** pool (measured in the count) and the **marginating** pool. Exercise, adrenaline and steroids cause demargination (rapid rise in count); infection and G-CSF mobilise the **marrow storage pool**, often with a left shift.

## Simplified explanation

The storage pool waits in the marrow. The marginating pool is already in the blood but stuck to vessel walls.
hint: Where is each pool located?

body: In two sentences explain the role of Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase in the phagocytic function of neutrophils.
answer:
G6PD (hexose monophosphate shunt) generates the **NADPH** that **NADPH oxidase** uses to reduce oxygen to **superoxide** during the **respiratory burst**. Superoxide is converted to H₂O₂ and, by myeloperoxidase, to **hypochlorous acid**, which kill ingested microbes (NADPH also protects the neutrophil via glutathione).

> [!answer]
> G6PD supplies NADPH for NADPH oxidase → reactive oxygen species for microbial killing.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Phagocytosis triggers assembly of NADPH oxidase (gp91phox/p22phox with p47, p67, p40phox, Rac). Severe G6PD deficiency (<5% activity) can impair the respiratory burst and mimic chronic granulomatous disease.

## Simplified explanation

G6PD makes NADPH, the fuel the neutrophil burns to make bleach-like chemicals that kill bacteria.
hint: Link G6PD → NADPH → respiratory burst.

body: State two conditions that can cause "right shift" in peripheral blood neutrophil count.
answer:
Any two: **vitamin B12 deficiency**, **folate deficiency** (megaloblastic anaemia), **uraemia/chronic renal failure**, iron deficiency, drugs (methotrexate, hydroxycarbamide), hereditary hypersegmentation.

> [!answer]
> Vitamin B12 deficiency and folate deficiency.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **right shift** means increased hypersegmented neutrophils (≥5 lobes). Impaired DNA synthesis in megaloblastic anaemia delays nuclear maturation and gives hypersegmentation, often before macrocytosis appears.

## Simplified explanation

Right shift (too many lobes) is typical of B12 or folate deficiency.
hint: Right shift = hypersegmentation.

body: In two sentences, explain why neutrophil alkaline phosphatase score go up in inflammation.
answer:
In inflammation, cytokines such as **G-CSF and IFN-γ** activate neutrophils and stimulate synthesis of alkaline phosphatase in their secretory vesicles, and young activated neutrophils are released from the marrow. Therefore more neutrophils stain strongly for ALP, and the **NAP score rises**.

> [!answer]
> Cytokine (G-CSF) activation increases neutrophil ALP synthesis, so NAP score rises.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

NAP is scored by staining 100 neutrophils (0–4+) with naphthol AS phosphate and a diazonium salt (normal ~20–100). G-CSF is a strong inducer of NAP, so the score is high in infection, inflammation and G-CSF therapy, and low in CML (BCR-ABL1 neutrophils).

## Simplified explanation

Inflammation signals switch neutrophils on, and active neutrophils make more alkaline phosphatase.
hint: G-CSF induces NAP.

body: In one sentence, state the effect of excess IL-5 on haematopoietic cells production.
answer:
Excess IL-5 stimulates **eosinophil** production, differentiation, activation and survival, causing **eosinophilia**.

> [!answer]
> Eosinophilia.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

IL-5 (from Th2 cells, ILC2s) acts on IL-5Rα on eosinophil progenitors and mature eosinophils; it also supports B-cell IgA responses. Anti-IL-5 (mepolizumab) reduces eosinophils in eosinophilic asthma.

## Simplified explanation

Too much IL-5 means too many eosinophils.
hint: IL-5 is the eosinophil cytokine.

body: State three (3) issues/conditions that constitute medical negligence in phlebotomy.
answer:
Any three:

- Failure to **identify the patient** correctly or **mislabelling** the sample.
- Drawing blood **without informed consent** (or against a refusal).
- **Injury** from poor technique: nerve injury, arterial puncture, large haematoma, repeated probing.
- Failure to follow **aseptic technique**/reuse of needles, causing infection; needle-stick or sharps-disposal failures.
- Leaving the patient **unattended** (fainting, falls) or ignoring complaints of pain.
- Drawing from an inappropriate site (arm with IV line, mastectomy side, fistula).

> [!answer]
> e.g. wrong patient/mislabelling, no consent, injury from improper technique.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Negligence = breach of the duty of care that causes harm. Phlebotomy standards (CLSI GP41, WHO guidelines) cover two-identifier patient identification, consent, site selection, tourniquet time <1 min, asepsis, safe sharps disposal and monitoring the patient.

## Simplified explanation

Negligence means not doing what a careful phlebotomist should: wrong patient, no consent, causing injury or infection.
hint: Think identification, consent, injury, infection.

body:
Explain why the following sites are not suitable for dermal puncture in adults:

(i) heel

(ii) thumb
answer:
- **(i) Heel:** in adults the heel skin is **thick and calloused**, so it is hard to obtain free-flowing blood; heel puncture is designed for infants. Deep puncture risks hitting the **calcaneus** (osteomyelitis).
- **(ii) Thumb:** it has a **pulse** (risk of arterial blood), **thick calloused skin**, and the bone is close to the surface, giving a poor and painful sample.

> [!answer]
> Heel: thick skin and risk to bone; recommended only for infants. Thumb: has a pulse and thick skin.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Adult capillary puncture uses the palmar surface of the distal phalanx of the **middle or ring finger** of the non-dominant hand, perpendicular to the fingerprint lines. Avoid the thumb (pulse, thick skin), index finger (calloused, sensitive), little finger (thin tissue over bone). Heel puncture is restricted to infants <1 year, on the medial or lateral plantar surface.

## Simplified explanation

In adults, use the middle or ring finger. The heel skin is too thick and the thumb has a pulse.
hint: Which fingers are recommended for adults?

body: In what instance will a blood culture be requested STAT?
answer:
When **sepsis/septicaemia (bacteraemia)** is suspected and treatment is urgent, e.g. a patient with **fever with chills/rigors**, hypotension or septic shock, suspected **meningitis**, **infective endocarditis**, **neonatal sepsis**, or **febrile neutropenia**, ideally **before antibiotics are started** (or at the temperature spike).

> [!answer]
> Suspected septicaemia (e.g. fever with rigors, septic shock), before the first dose of antibiotics.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

STAT = immediately. Blood cultures guide life-saving antimicrobial therapy, so they are drawn at once when sepsis is suspected, ideally 2–3 sets from separate sites with strict aseptic technique, before antibiotics (which reduce yield), and without delaying empirical treatment.

## Simplified explanation

If a patient may have a blood infection, especially before antibiotics start, blood culture is taken right away.
hint: Why would delay be dangerous?

body: Mrs. Mensah was rushed to the hospital during your night shift, unconscious. As the laboratory scientist on duty, a request form was sent by the doctor through a nurse to you to perform certain blood tests on Mrs. Mensah. How would you seek her consent to perform the procedure?
answer:
- An unconscious patient cannot give consent, so in an **emergency** the procedure proceeds on **implied consent** (presumed that a reasonable person would agree to life-saving investigations).
- Where possible, obtain consent from the **next of kin/legal guardian** or relatives present, and rely on the **doctor's request/authorisation** (documented on the form).
- **Document** the circumstances, and inform the patient once she regains consciousness.

> [!answer]
> Implied (emergency) consent, with consent sought from next of kin/guardian where available, and documentation.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Consent may be expressed (verbal/written) or implied. For incapacitated patients in an emergency, the doctrine of necessity/implied consent applies; surrogate consent from next of kin or legal representative is sought when available. The phlebotomist should still identify the patient (wristband, nurse confirmation) and record how consent was obtained.

## Simplified explanation

If the patient can't speak, treat it as emergency (implied) consent, ask the family if present, and write it down.
hint: Who can consent for an unconscious patient?

body: Critically enumerate the procedural steps you would take to ensure reliability of tests to be undertaken on a patient suspected to have cold agglutinins if you are required to draw blood sample.
answer:
1. **Pre-warm** the collection tubes (and syringe/needle) to **37 °C**.
2. If possible warm the patient's arm/limb before venepuncture.
3. Collect the sample and immediately place it in a **37 °C** water bath or warm flask/insulated container.
4. **Transport at 37 °C** without delay; do not refrigerate.
5. For serum tests, allow clotting and **separate serum at 37 °C**; for FBC, **incubate the EDTA sample at 37 °C** (~15–30 min) and analyse while warm (repeat after warming if MCHC is high).
6. Prepare blood films from the warmed sample.

> [!answer]
> Keep the sample at 37 °C from collection to separation/analysis (pre-warmed tubes, warm transport, warm separation/analysis).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Cold agglutinins (usually IgM anti-I) agglutinate red cells below 37 °C. In vitro agglutination gives a **falsely low RBC count and Hct**, **falsely high MCV and MCHC** (>370 g/L), and clumps on the film; for cold agglutinin titres, letting the sample cool before separation lets the antibody absorb onto red cells, giving a falsely low titre.

## Simplified explanation

Keep the blood warm (37 °C) the whole time, from the needle to the analyser, so the antibody can't clump the red cells.
hint: Cold antibodies act at low temperature.

body: State three adverse effects that storage of blood in EDTA for >6 hours (at room temperature) can have on haematological analyses.
answer:
Any three:

- **Red cell swelling**: rise in **MCV and PCV/Hct**, fall in MCHC.
- Morphological artefacts: **crenated/spherocytic red cells**, **neutrophil vacuolation**/pyknosis, **lobulated lymphocytes**, disintegrating cells (smear cells).
- **Platelet** swelling/clumping and change in platelet count and MPV.
- Falsely **low ESR**.
- Changes in WBC differential on analysers (degenerating neutrophils misclassified).

> [!answer]
> e.g. raised MCV/PCV, morphological artefacts in films, altered platelet count/ESR.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

ICSH recommends making films within 3 hours and running FBC within 6 hours (or within 24 h if stored at 4 °C). EDTA causes progressive red cell swelling and leucocyte degeneration; the ESR must be done within 4 hours (or 24 h at 4 °C).

## Simplified explanation

Old EDTA blood gives bigger red cells (higher MCV), messy-looking white cells, wrong platelet counts and a falsely low ESR.
hint: Think indices, morphology and ESR.

body: In not more than two (2) sentences, explain how blood sample for arterial blood gas measurements are to be transported to the laboratory.
answer:
The heparinised syringe should be **free of air bubbles**, **capped** (needle removed) and **mixed**, then transported **immediately** and analysed within ~15–30 minutes (at room temperature for plastic syringes, or on **ice/iced water** for glass syringes if delay is expected) to stop cellular metabolism changing pO₂, pCO₂ and pH.

> [!answer]
> Anaerobically (no air, capped), promptly, cooled if delay is expected.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Air bubbles equilibrate with the sample (raising pO₂ towards ~150 mmHg and lowering pCO₂). Leucocytes and platelets keep consuming O₂ and producing CO₂/lactate, so pO₂ and pH fall with time. Plastic syringes are gas-permeable, so icing them is no longer recommended; analyse within 30 min.

## Simplified explanation

Keep air out, cap the syringe and get it to the lab fast (on ice if there will be a delay).
hint: Air and time both change blood gases.

body: A ward nurse brought a venous blood sample that had been drawn from patient Asante Apietu for full blood count estimation. The MLS at the reception rejected the sample and requested a fresh sample to be drawn. State three situations which might have informed rejection of the specimen.
answer:
Any three:

- Sample **unlabelled or mislabelled**, or details not matching the request form.
- Sample **clotted** (or contains microclots).
- Sample **haemolysed**.
- **Wrong container/anticoagulant** (e.g. citrate or plain tube for FBC).
- **Under- or over-filled** tube (wrong blood:EDTA ratio) or insufficient volume.
- Sample **too old**/delayed in transport, or leaking container.

> [!answer]
> e.g. mislabelled, clotted, haemolysed (also wrong tube, wrong volume, delayed).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Specimen rejection criteria are part of the laboratory's pre-analytical quality system (ISO 15189): patient identification errors, inappropriate container, insufficient/excess volume, clotting, haemolysis, lipaemia (for some tests), excessive delay or inappropriate storage.

## Simplified explanation

A lab rejects a sample if it isn't labelled properly, is clotted or haemolysed, or is in the wrong tube or amount.
hint: Identification, container, sample quality.

body:
The standard EDTA-to-blood anticoagulant ratio is 2 mg/ml. An MLS took 3 ml of blood into EDTA tube that contained 4 mg EDTA.

(I) Explain (with reasons) whether this is an appropriate blood-to-anticoagulant ratio.

(II) State two impact of this blood-to-anticoagulant ratio on haematological analyses.
answer:
**(I)** Not appropriate: 4 mg EDTA ÷ 3 ml = **1.33 mg/ml**, below the 2 mg/ml standard. The tube is **overfilled** (4 mg should take **2 ml** of blood), so there is **too little anticoagulant** for the volume of blood.

**(II)** Any two:

- Incomplete anticoagulation → **microclots/clots**, with **falsely low platelet count** (and low WBC/RBC counts).
- **Platelet clumping/aggregation** (pseudothrombocytopenia, falsely raised WBC from clumps).
- Clots may **block the analyser**.
- Unreliable results; sample may have to be rejected.

> [!answer]
> 1.33 mg/ml: too little EDTA (should be 2 ml blood). Effects: microclots → low platelet/cell counts, analyser blockage.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

EDTA chelates Ca²⁺ to prevent clotting; the ICSH-recommended concentration is ~1.5–2.2 mg/ml blood. Too **little** EDTA (overfilled tube) → clotting and platelet clumping. Too **much** EDTA (underfilled tube) → red cell shrinkage (low PCV, high MCHC), and degenerative changes in leucocytes and platelets.

## Simplified explanation

4 mg of EDTA is enough for only 2 ml of blood. With 3 ml, there isn't enough anticoagulant, so tiny clots form and counts (especially platelets) come out falsely low.
hint: Divide the EDTA by the blood volume.
